{"docket_number": "83-18", "additional_docket_numbers": null, "term": "1983", "first_party": "Dun & Bradstreet, Inc.", "first_party_label": "Petitioner", "second_party": "Greenmoss Builders, Inc.", "second_party_label": "Respondent", "manner_of_jurisdiction": "Writ of certiorari", "lower_court": "Vermont Supreme Court", "argued": ["1984-03-21T06:00:00Z"], "question": "

If a trial judge does not instruct the jury to only award punitive damages caused by intentional slander or reckless conduct, can a jury still award punitive damages to a plaintiff defamed by private speech?

", "facts_of_the_case": "

Dun and Bradstreet, a credit reporting agency, mistakenly reported to some of its subscribers that the construction contractor Greenmoss Builders had voluntarily filed for bankruptcy. The president of Greenmoss quickly learned about the erroneous report, requested Bradstreet to correct its error, and asked for the list of subscribers who received the report. Bradstreet refused to release the names on the list, but issued a correction to its five subscribers who received the original report. The correction stated that actually a former employee of Greenmoss had filed for bankruptcy and that Greenmoss Builders "continued in business as usual." Greenmoss was dissatisfied with the correction and again asked for the list. When Bradstreet refused a second time, Greenmoss filed suit against it for defamation in a Vermont state court. The court discovered that a 17-year-old high student interning for Bradstreet had caused the error and the jury awarded $350,000 to Greenmoss in compensatory and punitive damages. Bradstreet claimed that contrary to the Supreme Court's ruling in Gertz v. Robert Welch, the trial judge told the jury that it could award punitive damages even if Bradford did not make mistakes intentionally or out of recklessness. The court granted Bradstreet's motion for retrial, but the Vermont Supreme Court ruled that Gertz only applied to cases involving defamation by the media.

", "conclusion": "

Yes. Justice Lewis Powell authored the opinion for a 5-4 court. Although the trial court correctly perceived that the trial judge's instructions did not satisfy the requirements of Gertz, the Court held that Gertz did not apply since the present case did not involve public speech. Instead the Court looked to apply the logic of Gertz to situations concerning private speech. The Court reasoned that laws regulating defamation suits aimed to "balance the State's interest in compensating private individuals for injury to their reputation against the First Amendment interest in protecting this type [Bradstreet's] of expression." Because the First Amendment offers less protection to private speech than to public speech, and especially less to speech "being solely motived by a desire for profit," damages caused by it can result in heavier penalties and broader conditions for convictions. Therefore states can allow the recovery of punitive damages in defamation cases involving private speech even when the perpetrator does not demonstrate "actual malice."

analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "We will hear arguments first this morning in Dun & Bradstreet against Green Moss Builders. Mr. Garrett, you may proceed whenever you're ready. Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court. This is a case about damages for defamation. The question presented is one that ten years ago this Court in Gertz v. Robert Welchink sought to answer. What is the proper accommodation between the law of defamation and the freedoms of speech and press protected by the First Amendment? The Gertz decision recognized two very important things. It recognized that the states have a substantial interest in protecting the reputations of its citizens. Also, it recognized that absent actual malice, the states have no interest in awarding either presumed or punitive damages, and that the First Amendment precludes such awards. In its holding, it accommodated these two competing interests, and it held that a private defamation plaintiff who establishes liability under a less demanding standard than the New York Times test of actual malice may only recover damages which compensate him for actual injury. It is these constitutional rules prohibiting awards of presumed and punitive damages absent calculated falsehood that Petitioner Dunn and Bradstreet asked this Court to apply. We believe that Gertz properly considered the tension between First Amendment freedoms on the one hand and repudational interest on the other. Neither Green Moss Builders nor the Vermont Supreme Court advance any reason why the states have a greater interest in awarding presumed and punitive damages against a non-media defendant who speaks about business matters or matters about the arts than a media speaker. I'll give a definition of the difference between media and non-media. I can understand it clearly if a private individual writes a letter or makes a statement. That person as an individual is probably non-media. But what's your definition of non-media generally? Your Honor, I think that's the rub in this case when it comes to deciding constitutional limitations on presumed and punitive damages. Obviously, the media could be defined as one who uses a medium to communicate information. And Dunn and Bradstreet, much like a newspaper, does that. We hire reporters to obtain information which air subscribers will want. Now we have in Washington, I don't know how many, but I suppose it must be a great number of letters like the Kiplinger letter. It goes out every week or periodically, sometimes on a broad range of subjects, sometimes on a limited subject like labor law. Is that media or non-media? It seems to me, Your Honor, while the Kiplinger letter like Dunn and Bradstreet may not be considered the traditional media, it is certainly media in that it is an organization that communicates information to its readers which have a reason to know that. That issue before us, Counsel, you didn't bring that issue up here. The media, non-media issue? That's the very basis that the Vermont Supreme Court ruled against Dunn and Bradstreet in this case. I know, but they held that you were non-media. They said... Did you challenge that in your petition, Mr. Scherzer? Oh, absolutely, Your Honor. Well, we did not... We have never taken the position, Your Honor, that we were the traditional media like newspapers. I mean, you're taking the position that you're media? We certainly take the position that we're media for the application of the Gertz rules on presumed impunitive damages. Well... Of course, your first question presented in the search, your area is, do the first and 14th amendments to the Constitution permit private plans to recover presumed compensatory damages are generally reliable against a non-media defendant? That is correct, Your Honor. As I said, we have never taken the position that Dunn and Bradstreet was part of the traditional media like the New York Times or CBS. But we certainly are media in the sense that we communicate information to air subscribers. The way to present the case to us is that let's assume that this is a non-media defendant and then does Gertz apply to non-media defendants? That's the question you put to us. That is correct, based on the... Do we have to get into whether Dunn and Bradstreet is or isn't a media defendant? Your Honor, I think it's quite... You say we don't, really, in this question. Well, I think it's quite correct that the constitutional prohibitions against presumed impunitive damages don't depend on the nature of the speaker or the subject matter of his speech. Right, right. I thought you thought in order to win your case you would have to convince us that Gertz applies to non-media defendants generally. Or... And I think that's your whole argument, too, and your brief. I think certainly that that would win the case for us, Your Honor. How do we reach that question if we don't know what a non-media defendant is? Well, I think that's the very problem in the case, Your Honor, that it would force the courts to go back to basically the Rosenblum ad hoc test to make determinations on who is and who is not the media. And I think the most important thing is that the rationale for the Gertz opinion simply does not depend on those kinds of distinctions. The states have no interest in awarding presumed impunitive damages absent actual malice. Against anyone? Against anyone. Right, right. That's your argument. And I... that is your argument, but I would suggest to the court that if the court is concerned that a media, non-media distinction should be made in certain contexts, this is not the one to make it in. There may be areas where that would be appropriate, but not in connection with the awards of presumed impunitive damages. But I thought your position was and is that it makes no difference who the plaintiff and who the defendant may be. If you sued me for liable, for example, the rule would be the same in your view. That's correct. We do not believe that an individual could be awarded presumed damages because that simply is not proper for the states. Right. And while we're getting at definitions, how do you define the difference between presumed and punitive damages? Your Honor, in traditional libel law, presumed damages really took the place of compensatory or actual damages. Punitive damages, on the other hand, were more of a punitive punishment measure. The problem in the cases, however, Your Honor, is that they're both used selectively to punish unpopular speakers. And I think it's very difficult to make a distinction when it comes to the effect of presumed and punitive damages on First Amendment activities. If you went back to the common law perception of presumed damages as being a substitute for actual damages, would that make a difference in your submission? No, Your Honor, because the only rule we're asking for is that the jury not be told that damages are presumed. We are fully prepared to live with the Goertz rule that says a defamation plaintiff may recover all injuries, excuse me, all damages for his actual injury. Will you sort of itemize what they may be? Well, for example... Under the Goertz formula. Under the Goertz formula, for an individual it may be humiliation, it may be embarrassment, it may be damage to reputation. It's a number of intangible things. For other plaintiffs, such as a corporation, it could be lost profits, it could be an inability to borrow money which affected the business, it could be the business's reputation. Yes, but you agree with Goertz that you don't have to prove actual pecuniary laws. I agree with Goertz that for the private individual he not prove actual pecuniary laws. And I think the Goertz rule says that you don't have to give a damaged figure. But even with respect to a corporation, there could be a loss of reputation as in this case. I say there could be a loss of a corporation's reputation. In this case, for example, the problem was a report of bankruptcy which doesn't do a corporation very much good, does it? Go ahead, Don. That's correct, Your Honor. The distinction in this case, rather than proving a quantum of damages, it's proving a causal connection between the fact that the report was issued and the individuals to whom it was issued to took any action adverse to Greenwald. Would you agree that any damages can be proved in this case? Based on the evidence of the lower court or could be? Could be. Oh, yes. I think damages could be proved. But what the jury could not be told was damages are presumed. I think that is the single rule that we ask this court to apply, as well as the prohibition against punitive damages. Do punitive damages say the same purpose as presumed damages? I assume not, but I'd like to know what you think. Your Honor, traditionally, punitive damages have been used to deter conduct. That's the rationale behind them. I guess, technically speaking, there is a difference between presumed and punitive damages as far as their effect. However, I think in the area of libel law, they both have the same effect. When a jury is told that you may presume damage, we believe that by the very nature of that charge, you chill First Amendment activity. A punitive damage award is a private fine. Do you agree with that? That's correct, Your Honor. And it's a private fine, unfortunately, based on various state standards which do not give juries much guidance. And we think in the area of libel law, the actual malice test focuses on the conduct of the defendant at the time he made the publication. And that is the correct test. Would your view, and this is the last question I'll ask you for a while, I think. Would your view of punitive damages applied to a garden variety tort case other than the tort of libel, where compensatory damages can be proved? Well, Your Honor, I think as the— That's not the question before you, but I'm interested in your perception of the purpose and range of punitive damages. Well, Your Honor, I think as the court indicated in Smith v. Wade, punitive damage is a very troublesome area in the law. You know, I'm reminded of what Justice Rehnquist wrote in that decision from Oliver Wendell Holmes. You know, a dog can tell the difference between accidentally kicked and being stomped every day. Well, if you stomp somebody every day, you're going to chill their activity. And the real problem is that punitive damages often shield beneficial conduct, that they're too far ranging, and that's a very difficult problem in the law, separate and apart from the libel area, Your Honor. You're having private parties impose punitive fines. That's correct. Without due process of law? It's a close question depending on the standards. I do not believe that's the case in the First Amendment test of actual malice. But when punitive damages, for example, can be given, as they were in this case, Your Honor, for something called reckless disregards of the interests of the plaintiff, that's a fairly broad-ranging state privilege. Against Sullivan? I'm sorry, Your Honor? Isn't the reckless disregard from Sullivan? No, Your Honor. The lower court was reckless disregard for the interests of the plaintiff. That language, that language is... Oh, certainly reckless disregard, but it's for a different interest. Reckless disregard for the truth in New York Times versus something called reckless disregard for the interests of the plaintiff. We believe, Your Honor, that the facts of this case highlight the very concern that the court recognized in Gertz. Presumed in punitive damages awarded by juries to punish an unpopular speaker. Here, we sent a special notice to five people. It was corrected shortly thereafter. None of these individuals were a customer of green moss. As I said, we sent the retraction immediately. The plaintiff called not one recipient of the notice to the stand to testify. There was no causal connection between our report and the alleged lost profits of the company. What occurred was a jury instruction that allowed the jury to award unlimited amounts of presumed impunitive damages. The jury were instructed that this was a case of libel per se and that damage and loss were conclusively presumed. The court instructed the jury that it could award presumed or exemplary damages based on something called actual malice, which was never defined for the jury. The lower court found that its jury charge was misleading and granted Dun & Bradstreet a new trial. The Supreme Court of Vermont reversed, finding that Dun & Bradstreet was a non-media defendant and that non-media defendant a state could award presumed and punitive damages. What the Vermont Supreme Court did was focus on the status of D and B on what it termed as a non-media defendant and the content of its message. The Vermont Supreme Court fails to identify any state interest which justifies awards of presumed or punitive damages against Dun & Bradstreet any more than against a small newspaper or local radio station. The issue in this case simply put is this. If the Burlington Vermont publishes Green Moss is bankrupt, they are entitled to a constitutional instruction that precludes the awards of presumed impunitive damages. Yet if Dun & Bradstreet publishes that same information to its subscribers because they want to know, they are not entitled to that constitutional protection. The law is entitled to a constitutional protection that no damages can be awarded even if they are approved without proof of fault? Yes, we believe that we are entitled to the fault standard. And even Sunward that filed an amicus brief in this case said we are entitled at least to the fault standard. In this case, we do not contest fault. I suppose if you say that the Gertz rules don't apply against non-media defendants, the fault requirement would disappear too, I suppose. That's correct. In other words, if that were the case, Your Honor, a plaintiff could merely prove falsity of the report and go to the jury on damage. Go back to the old rule before. That's absolutely correct, Your Honor. Mr. Garrett, you suggest there can't be a difference between your client and a newspaper of general circulation. Supposing there were a statute that said credit reporting agencies that report a bankruptcy must, in addition, state the source of their information. Would that be constitutional? I don't suppose you could compel a newspaper to do that, but could you compel a credit reporting agency to do that? Your Honor, I think that the Miami Herald case answered for the newspapers. Right. I see differences, Your Honor, in connection with requiring credit reporting agencies, for example, the Fair Credit Reporting Act, from requiring disclosures and from requiring identity of information. To me, that is much different than a warning of presumed or punitive damages. And I think there's arguably a state and federal interest in the former, but not the latter. I agree. It is, however, quite clearly. It would be a regulation of content. And you would, nevertheless, say it would be permissible. I think regulation of content in certain instances like that could be permissible. I do think there's a distinction, Your Honor, in regulating awards of presumed and punitive damages based on the subject matter of the speech. In fact... Supposing I went one step further and my statute said that if you fail to do this, you should be subject to a $100 fine, purely punitive. Okay. And I think the difference in that, Your Honor, is you're not regulating the speech so much as you are the violation of a federal or state statute. And to me, that's different because, in my case, you're punishing speech. And I think, to go further with your question, Justice Stevens, the actual malice test of New York Times, and said further in Time, Inc. versus Firestone, was designed to avoid looking at the subject matter. You focused on misconduct. And I believe in Time, Inc. versus Firestone, the court acknowledged that too often when we look at subject matter, we skew the balance of the state interest on the one hand and the First Amendment on the other. And that's what the Vermont Supreme Court did in this case. It skewed the balance between free speech and state interest in reputation. It allowed the jury to compensate Green Moss beyond actual injury. It allowed the jury to punish Dunning-Brad Street, not because of any showing of calculated falsehood, but simply because after special notice turned out to be false. The First Amendment rests on the assumption of the widest possible dissemination of information from diverse sources. There's no reason to permit defamed private plaintiffs in a business context or defamed private plaintiffs by a non-media defendant windfall damages, because the effect is still the same. It's punishment. The prospect of discretionary awards have a chilling effect on what is published and when, whether media or non-media. Are you saying that presumed damages are a punishment? That certainly wasn't the basis in which the libel law developed that. It was the idea that the kinds of injuries you suffer in libel to reputation are not easily quantified in dollar amounts, isn't it? That's certainly historical. But, Your Honor, in looking at the jury verdicts, the Sunward case that filed in the Meekersbury, $3.5 million, when a jury is allowed to give damages without any regard to actual injury, that can be punishment, because it can be used to punish an unpopular speaker. Well, you say without any regard to actual injury. That's correct. Are you saying, then, that damage or ruining a reputation is not actual injury? Your Honor, that certainly could be actual injury. But, in the business context that we're in, it's no different from proving damages for a corporation for breach of contract or any other thing. You have to come into court with competent evidence. Well, but Gertz says you don't have to itemize dollar amounts, like pain and suffering, medicals, and that sort of thing. So, I mean, if you're going to have damages to reputation, it's going to be a lump sum type of thing that you can't relate to dollar testimony, isn't it? That's correct, Your Honor. But you still have to prove a causal connection between the publication of the defamatory words and the damage. Well, surely, but the fact... And that's what was lacking in this case. Well, it may be lacking in this case, but your suggestion that any award of $3.5 million for damages to reputation must be punishment, because it couldn't possibly have been amounted to that much, I would think would depend very much on the facts and circumstances of each case. Your Honor, I would agree with you if no presumed damage charge is given. But when the jury is told damages are presumed, and then this court or any court reviewing that has no idea what the jury based it on. And that's the problem with the presumed damage charge. There ought to be proof of some damage. There ought to be proof of actual injury. Well, all right. Let's assume that you can... Let's assume you get one witness come in and say, I think less than I've done on Bradstreet than I did before. As a matter of fact, I've canceled my subscription, which ought to injure them. And, uh... I know, I know. But nevertheless, there's proof... There's proof... There's proof of an injury. And, uh... Now, is that enough for you? Or would you have to quantify it? I think that a... That a plaintiff could come into court with a witness and say, my injury or my reputation has been injured. No dollar figure has to be assigned to that. But once an injury is proved, it doesn't mean that you can presume any amount of damages based on that. You may get damages which naturally flow from the damage to reputation. And you really think that they're going to... You have to do the impossible, prove the amount of the damage. No, sir. I did not suggest that, Your Honor. I'm merely suggesting that once the fact that you have one witness that says the plaintiff's reputation has been damaged... Well, he's proved injury. That's correct. And he may get all the damages for that actual injury. Let me put this to you. Suppose the witness that Justice White has postulated was one of the directors of the bank where Green Moss did business. And under examination, he said that this was discussed for a half hour at a meeting of the bank's board of directors and that the conclusion was from the president summing it up, from now on keep a very close eye on Green Moss builders because there's something wrong here. Now, is that a damage or is it not? Yes, sir. Your Honor, it's very difficult for me to say that that's a damage to a corporation. And that's why, perhaps, that certain damages can be presumed. Your Honor, I don't believe that's what the law said in Gertz. Certainly before that it did. I'm talking about the law of Delaware. The common law of the states has been... The common law of the states certainly has been... The common law of the states certainly has been... The presumption of damage. Because this injury is so difficult to measure that there is a presumption that is permitted by the jury. That certainly was the common law prior to Gertz, Your Honor. That's correct. Well, suppose the president... Well, if somebody comes in and says that you, I'm a corporation doing business, and you have circulated a statement that I'm bankrupt, isn't that damage per se without more? No, Your Honor, I don't believe it is. Well, let's put it this way. It won't help it. It may not help them, but it may not hurt them either, Your Honor. You mean, would you do business with a bankrupt corporation? If I got a notice that someone was bankrupt, and I knew it was wrong, and it didn't affect my relationship, I don't believe that makes any difference for them. Would you buy any stock in that corporation? If I knew it was incorrect, certainly, Your Honor. Oh, I didn't say incorrect. Would you buy stock in a bankrupt corporation? No, Your Honor. Well, then that's an injury, isn't it? If the fact of the publication resulted in that. Huh? If the fact of the publication resulted in that effect. Well, I asked you, would you buy stock in a corporation that Dunn and Bradstreet said was bankrupt? No, sir, I would not. Well, that's sort of an injury, isn't it? If, in fact, it was incorrectly reported and that was the result, yes, that would be a quantifiable injury, Your Honor. That is correct, Your Honor, if, in fact, that occurred. Well, what's this case? This case is, there was no cause, the jury was allowed to presume damages and there was no causal. Well, don't, isn't this presuming what I just said? No, Your Honor, they were told damages are presumed, period. And there was no causal connection by evidence between the publication of the report and any action by the people that received it. No showing that anyone did anything toward Green Moss as a result of that report. But what was the purpose of Dunn and Bradstreet's publication? To inform its subscribers about an event which it thought was correct. That's the truth. That is correct. That's the truth. And it was a lie. That is correct. And, Your Honor, it's no different than the lie in every libel case. It's no different than the lie in Gert versus Welch. If a libel case is not done, you can get punitive damages. If you meet a certain standard, that's correct, Your Honor. That's right. Is it the same, really? They pick up the telephone, call the clerk of the court where the bankruptcy was asserted to have been filed, and said, has Green Moss builders filed or has someone sought a bankruptcy on them? Very easy to find out the truth, the fact, isn't it? That, Your Honor, this is verifiable information, no matter whether it's published in Dunn and Bradstreet or a local newspaper. It's a matter of public recognition. Well, it's a lot easier than what a newspaper is frequently confronted with. I would not think so, Your Honor, when it comes to reporting matters of public record. Both Dunn and Bradstreet and the newspapers can make mistakes. They're reading the same document. And if I might, I'd like to reserve the remainder of my time for a vote. Mr. Howland. Thank you, Your Honor. Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the court. Before commencing my argument, I'd like to correct what I think is not the evidence before this court. And I'd like to start by focusing on this correction report. The correction report, which was a very important part of this case, we say was worse than the actual report of the bankruptcy. In other words, we were focusing on the conduct of this defendant after the publication. The corrective report, we said, was more damaging in many respects because it left creditors with ambiguity. The second point that I want to correct is that Mr. Garrett tells you that there was no showing that anyone did anything at the bank with respect to the green moss builders. That's not what the evidence demonstrated. First, the evidence demonstrated that the specific loan request, and the Vermont Supreme Court found this, the specific loan request was immediately suspended. And we're talking about August in Vermont, when you have to start building. Secondly, in close temporal proximity to the report of the bankruptcy, a bank that had a perfectly good relationship with this construction company, all of a sudden told that construction company, not only will we deny that request for a loan, we'd like you to go somewhere else for all of your banking business. I don't think that it's credible to say that no one showed any injury, no one showed any harm resulting from the bankruptcy. Mr. Hammond, doesn't that merely establish the proposition that if you're required to prove actual injury, you'll be able to do so? No, Your Honor. How does that go to the question whether you need to prove actual injury? Your Honor, I think it focuses on the conduct of Dun & Bradstreet after the publication, which I think is a separate issue in this case. Again, I suggest it just means you can win the case if you have to go back and try it according to their theory. As far as Dun & Bradstreet's argument, their initial question before the court, I think there are two different starting points. To Dun & Bradstreet, the existence of full First Amendment protection for these credit reports is a given proposition. And I don't think that they identify or associate themselves with a recognized First Amendment interest in the area of defamation. On the contrary, they start with the proposition that the common law of defamation doesn't have legitimacy. If there's no full First Amendment interest that Dun & Bradstreet can point to in a defamation context, the court cannot reshape the common law because it feels the common law is imperfect or unwise. So in order to vessel itself… Well, Mr. Howman, did you really answer Justice Stevens' question? Could you prove actual damages here if you had to? In this case, I think we could prove actual damages. I think that… Do you think that most libel plaintiffs can prove actual damages if they have to? I think that the presumption is necessary to assist private plaintiffs to bridge several causation gaps. I think many private plaintiffs may be able to prove some form of actual injury. I'm thinking now about Mr. Gertz, who on retrial testified that he suffered emotional distress. What is the presumption? Yes. I think that the problem of quantifying the… Even if you… You could prove an injury, but to prove the extent of it would be extremely difficult, I suppose, without the aid of a presumption. Well, I think so, Your Honor. I think that that's where the common law has its most beneficial effects, because the intuition of the common law says that harm has occurred. And these presumptions assist the private plaintiff in demonstrating and getting to the jury the kind of harm. What is the presumption you contend is appropriate? Does it tell us the amount of damages? Is there any presumption that concerns the amount of damage? Or does the presumption really go to the fact of damage? I think the presumption goes to the fact of damage and not so much to the amount of the damage. And I really think the presumption… So that if you're able to prove the fact of damage independently, then you don't need the presumption. Your Honor, doesn't it depend, counsel, on a jury's evaluation of, in effect, punishment? How vicious, how bad was the libel or how mild and inconsequential was it? And if they think it was very vicious and very bad, they might give a large punitive damage, presumed damage. Or if they thought it was casual and inconsequential, they would give one dollar, as sometimes happened. That may be so, Your Honor. And that's more in connection with the punitive damage than presumed damage. Justice Seaton, I'd like to finish… Well, how do you distinguish punitive and presumed? Well, I think that in this case, for example, the presumed damages were equated with actual injury within the description utilized by the court in Gertz. This punitive damage has, if you will, the white knight or the private attorney general. What do you think this large verdict was? Presumed or punitive or both? Well, this verdict was separated. 50,000 was actual, 300,000 was punitive. The large part was, therefore, punitive, the deterrence aspect. If I may, I'd like to get back to the question that you posed. You talk about the presumption. Gertz doesn't talk about the presumption. What Gertz talks about is the presumption of substantial damages. There are many common law presumptions. And I don't think Gertz focused on all common law presumptions in the defamation context. The common law presumption that I'm focusing on here is the presumption of causation. And I think that's particularly important when a business libel is concerned. Because, as Mr. Gertz pointed out, there is a federal statute dealing with the Consumer Credit Reporting Act. But there is no federal or state statute dealing with business credit reports. Therefore, a bank, a creditor, does not have to talk with you about the reasons why your credit was rejected. The bank can simply say, and this was the testimony at the trial, the bank can simply say, we have no obligation to speak with you about it.
